onbIntroBody.message: Keep sites you don't want the address bar to suggest here instead of in your bookmarks bar. After every visit to one of them, Nightstand clears the matching browsing history.

onbIntroNote.message: This is the only screen that explains what Nightstand is for, so it's best to finish setup when no one else can see your screen.

onbPassHint.message: You'll unlock by typing the passphrase into the "Filter" box, so it's best if it looks like an ordinary filter term — a few words separated by spaces, say. Anyone who sees you typing into a filter box won't think twice.

errPassTooShort.message: The passphrase must be at least 4 characters

errPassLooksLikeCode.message: The passphrase can't have the same format as a recovery code

onbCodeBody.message: If you forget your passphrase, paste the recovery code into the filter box and press Enter to set a new one. The recovery code is shown only this once — write it down or store it in a password manager.

onbHowTitle.message: How to use it from now on

onbHowBody.message: From now on, clicking the icon opens a "Quick Links" tool. Type your passphrase into the filter box and press Enter to unlock. Closing the popup locks it again.

plainExportWarning.message: Anyone who can open this file can see every URL and title you've saved. The file also appears in the browser's download history. Export only when you really need to, and delete it as soon as you're done.

recoveryRotateBody.message: Once a new recovery code is generated, the old one stops working immediately. Backups exported with the old recovery code can still be opened with the passphrase from that time.

faqMatchLink.message: What's the difference between the two options?

faqMatchQ.message: What's the difference between "Whole site" and "This URL only"?

faqMatchIntro.message: Say the saved URL is example.com/docs/guide. Here's whether a later visit to each of these URLs gets deleted from history:

faqMarkDeleted.description: FAQ match table cell: this visit's history is deleted.

faqMarkKept.description: FAQ match table cell: this visit's history is kept.

faqMatchSite.message: Whole site: only the domain matters — path, protocol and port are ignored. Any page on this domain or any of its subdomains is deleted from history after you visit it. The parent domain (def.com for abc.def.com) and look-alike domains (such as evil-example.com) are not affected.

faqMatchExact.message: This URL only: deletes just this one address. The protocol (http or https), a leading www., anything after # and a trailing slash don't matter, but the parameters after ? must match exactly. The site's home page and its other pages stay in history, so the browser may still suggest the site when you type its domain into the address bar.

faqMatchWhen.message: When it cleans up: existing history is cleaned as soon as you add an entry; after that, each visit is deleted right away. On top of that, a catch-up sweep runs every 15 minutes and every time the browser starts. Cleaning works while locked too.

faqMatchTip.message: If you want the address bar to never suggest the site at all, choose "Whole site".

faqExtraLink.message: What are extra domains, and how do I find them?

faqExtraQ.message: What are "Extra domains", and how do I find the ones to add?

faqExtra1.message: Some sites send you to other domains: a dedicated payment page when you pay, or the video server's own address when you play a video (for example video.twimg.com). Those domains aren't part of the site itself, so "Whole site" doesn't cover them; their history stays behind and the address bar still suggests them.

faqExtra2.message: Add them to the entry's "Extra domains", one per line. Extra domains are always treated as "Whole site", including all subdomains, whichever option the entry itself uses: their existing browsing history and bookmarks are deleted when you save, and every later visit is deleted automatically, even while locked.

faqExtraFind1.message: Open chrome://history in the address bar (in Firefox, the History window: Ctrl+Shift+H on Windows, ⌘⇧H on a Mac) and search for:

faqExtraFind2.message: the site's domain, for example example.com — finds entries whose URL contains it;

faqExtraFind3.message: words from the site's name or page titles — pages on another domain often still carry the site's name in their title, even though the URL is a different domain.

faqExtraFind4.message: Look at the domain shown next to each result; any that differ from the site itself are the extra domains to add. You can also copy that entry's URL and paste it straight in — the domain is extracted when you save.

faqExtraTip.message: It's best to look before you add the entry: once it's saved, the site's own history is gone and only words in titles are left to search for. And don't add big everyday sites (such as google.com): all history for them and every subdomain would be deleted.

faqStoreQ.message: How is my data stored? Can it be cracked?

faqStore1.message: All data stays in this computer's browser and is never uploaded anywhere.

faqStore2.message: Your list (URLs, titles, extra domains) is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The key that decrypts it exists only in the memory of the unlocked popup; it's destroyed when the popup closes and is never written to disk.

faqStore3.message: Your passphrase and recovery code are each turned into a key with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations), and that key unlocks the list's key. The encryption itself can't realistically be broken; the only thing an attacker can go after is the passphrase.

faqStore4.message: One thing to be aware of: so that history can be cleaned while locked, the extension also keeps a match table of which sites to clean. It stores only salted hashes, so the URLs can't be read directly — but someone with your browser data could hash a list of common sites and compare, to confirm whether you added a well-known site; they can also see how many entries there are. Titles are not exposed this way.

faqStore5.message: Nightstand protects against bystanders: projecting, screen sharing, someone looking over your shoulder. It can't protect against someone with full control of this computer, and it has no effect on Google account activity, DNS or network-level records.

faqSecretQ.message: Where are my passphrase and recovery code stored?

faqSecret1.message: Nowhere: neither the text itself nor a "fingerprint" (hash) of it is stored. Nightstand itself doesn't know what they are.

faqSecret2.message: Think of it this way: all the browser stores is a locked safe with your list inside. Your passphrase and recovery code are the combinations to that safe — either one opens it.

faqSecret3.message: The safe doesn't know its own combination. When you unlock, Nightstand tries to open it with what you typed: if it opens, the passphrase was right; if it doesn't, it was wrong. That's why it can't tell you what you got wrong — it only knows the safe didn't open.

faqSecret4.message: Because your passphrase and recovery code aren't stored anywhere, they can't leak from Nightstand. The only way into the safe is to guess, one try at a time (brute force), so the longer the passphrase, the safer.

faqSecret5.message: The safe stays open only while the popup is open. Closing the popup locks it again, so you enter your passphrase every time you open it.

faqSecret6.message: Changing your passphrase just swaps one of the combinations; the recovery code keeps working. Generating a new recovery code makes the old one stop working immediately. The recovery code is shown only once, when it's generated.

faqSecret7.message: An exported backup file is a copy of this safe and opens with the passphrase or recovery code from when it was exported.

faqSecretWarn.message: Precisely because nothing is stored, no one can recover a forgotten passphrase — only the recovery code can open the safe. Lose both, and the list can never be opened again.
